text: You already know the Administrator's job and the Developer's job from earlier in this path. This lesson draws the real line between those two roles and a third one: the Technical Architect.

An Administrator configures and maintains the platform within established patterns — users, groups, ACLs, notifications, update sets. A Developer builds features inside a container someone else defined — a flow, a widget, a scoped app. A Technical Architect decides the shape of that container itself: single instance or multiple, which integration pattern every future integration must follow, what data model every future app has to respect. Same instance, three genuinely different jobs.

It's tempting to think architect just means the hardest technical work. That's wrong. A developer might write code that's technically harder than anything an architect writes that week. The real boundary is consequence and reversibility. Choosing REST versus IntegrationHub for one integration, local to that integration, is a developer call. Choosing the pattern every future integration on the platform must follow is an architect call — because reversing it means re-touching every integration built under the old rule.

Design work is the visible part of the job, but real responsibility goes further. Architects lead design review — not redoing other people's work, but catching a choice that looks fine locally and breaks a platform-wide constraint. They set technical standards other teams are expected to follow without the architect touching their work directly. They mentor admins and developers into architectural judgment by explaining why a standard exists. And they carry accountability over time: if a decision made this year causes real pain in three years, the architect who made that call owns that outcome, long after the original project closed.

This course sits at the top of a thirteen-course path, and it assumes everything you've already learned as an admin and a developer. What it teaches next is how to weigh architectural tradeoffs and own their consequences — starting with a realistic look at the actual CTA credential.
